I've sat down with 10 consulting founders this year.

Almost none of them has a team.

The Gulf consulting market is set to grow 13% this year, according to Source Global Research. 

You'd expect the firms winning that work to be hiring. Plenty of them aren't.

Many are boutiques started by ex-MBB people I used to sit next to on projects.

For a lot of these firms, payroll is close to zero. AI handles the benchmarking and the first pass of analysis. Then one or two senior independents sit with the client and make the calls that a model can't.

Work that used to need a full pyramid now ships with two people and a stack of agents.

What surprised me is where it gets hard. 

With a team of two, each person has to be right. There's no associate layer to absorb a weak hire, and no bench to pull from when a client adds scope.

That's the gap we fill for several of them. 

We find the senior person, contract them, handle visas and admin, and put profiles in front of the founder within 48 hours.

If you run a lean firm, which is harder to find right now: the next client, or the person you'd trust in front of them?

---

I'm Michael Mudau, COO at Sharp Minds. I place fractional talent and consulting leaders into startups and government entities across the GCC.

Follow for more.

September Market
 
If you work in life sciences technology and you've noticed things going a bit quiet over the last six weeks, that's about to change.
 
September is consistently one of the most active hiring months in pharma and biotech, and this year the evidence suggests it's going to be particularly busy.
 
Life sciences hiring doesn't follow the same patterns as most industries. Q1 and Q3 consistently see the highest activity spikes, driven by conference seasons, funding announcements and programmes restarting after summer. The Q3 surge effectively starts the first week of September and it happens fast.
 
The context in 2026 makes this more significant than usual. The sector added roughly 100,000 jobs between late 2024 and mid-2026, with growth concentrated in biotech, AI-enabled R&D and digital manufacturing. Oncology alone attracted over 14 billion dollars in VC funding last year. That money turns into headcount and technology programmes, and those programmes need specialist resource.
 
At the same time, life sciences tech unemployment remains below 2 percent. The pool of genuinely experienced SAP, data and AI specialists with regulated environment experience has not grown at anything like the rate that demand has. When September hiring accelerates, that gap becomes very visible very quickly.
 
What this means in practice is straightforward. Candidates who are between contracts or thinking about a move should be having conversations now, not in three weeks. The best roles in September tend to go to people who were already in discussion in August.
 
And for hiring managers with roles to fill, if you've been waiting until everyone is back to start the process, you're already slightly behind.

Choosing the wrong AI agency is a compounding liability.

Because it sets the data architecture every future build relies on.

I've spent the last year auditing broken AI setups across the US and UK. You are likely sitting on a stack of proposals right now from firms promising to fix your operations.

The issue is most of those firms are just selling expensive advisory retainers. They hand you a 40-page roadmap. They map out a theoretical future. Then the contract ends and your head isn't even above water yet bc you still have to hire somebody else to actually build the system.

You need an implementation partner, not a theorist.

Here is exactly how you separate the two before you sign anything.

1/ Audit before tooling (if they pitch a platform before mapping your workflow, they are optimizing for their vendor relationships instead of your business)

2/ Retention over logos (tech partnerships are meaningless. ask for their 12-month client retention rate bc people only keep paying when the system finds or saves them actual money)

3/ Hard metrics upfront (if they won't define the reporting cadence and success metrics before the contract is signed, they are positioning themselves to make up the results later)

4/ Diagnosis into build (if they don't physically deploy the automation, walk away. a strategy document is useless to a 50-person company with no internal engineering team)

I've built over 200 of these systems and the math is always the same.

The cost of ripping out a bad AI foundation is ~3x the cost of just hiring a builder in the first place.

Read this aptly named article, "AI has broken Hiring" and it is something that I have been experiencing firsthand. 

AI has made every resume sound the same. I'm hiring a Sales Manager right now and one of the ATS shortlisted applicants is a stock controller. Good ATS match, right keywords, clean formatting. Looks like a top fit on paper. 

Here's the tell though, Half of the applicants for this role, regardless of actual background in sales have some version of the line "owned full P&L" on their resume. Like how? You are working in sales. Did you also own COGS? Vendor contracts? Pricing? P&L ownership means something specific and you don't get there by osmosis from hitting a quota. 

We are not shortlisting resumes that read like this and lack authenticity. Not because AI-assisted writing is banned, everyone uses these tools to some degree. Here's the thing, when a resume is built to match a JD instead of describing what you actually did, it stops telling us anything. 

So, if you are applying for the Sales manager role, tell us what you were actually responsible for. That's still the fastest way to stand out. Always has been.

Twelve months ago, a UK Forward Deployed Engineer contract went for about £700/day.
 
Right now it's closer to £850.
 
That jump tells you something the "FDE is an AI lab thing" narrative misses: this market has broken out of the labs and startups, and it's happening in the UK specifically, not just the US.
 
Where we're seeing the UK demand is actually coming from right now:
 
Financial services - firms here are burning through AI pilots that never make it to production, and paying for engineers who can actually get the thing live rather than another PoC.
 
Legal & compliance, life sciences - document review, clinical data, regulatory systems. Unglamorous, high-stakes, and hiring.
 
Defence & public sector - Palantir's own UK Government Deployment Strategist role is a good marker here; this isn't a private-sector-only trend.
 
The consultancies - EY launched a dedicated FDE track in April. Where Deloitte and Accenture go, the rest of the Big 4/6 usually follow. FDE is becoming a service line, not just a job title.
 
One structural detail worth knowing if you're hiring or contracting in this space: most of these UK roles are going out Outside IR35 - the work is genuinely outcome-driven rather than supervised delivery, which is exactly the kind of engagement that holds up under scrutiny.
 
There are roughly 220 FDE roles live in London right now on the major boards alone. This isn't a niche any more - it's a sector.

Stop hiring a Country Manager for France.

The conversation we have most often with foreign founders at Talma AI starts like this: "We're opening France. We need a Country Manager."

Then we ask three questions.
French revenue today? Zero.
Pipeline? Not yet.
What will this person do in their first 90 days? Calls, demos, follow-ups.

That's not a Country Manager. That's a seller.

Hire the title too early and here's what you get:
 → €140K OTE, close to €200K fully loaded
 → Someone who wants to build a team, not book meetings
 → A 4-month probation that ends before the first deal closes

And France adds its own surprises:
 → Commission plan written in English? Unenforceable.
 → Seller closing deals from Paris through an EOR? You may still owe French corporate tax.
 → Found the perfect candidate? They start in 3 months.

The right sequence:
 No French revenue → founding Account Executive
 First customers → Head of Sales
 Real local P&L → Country Manager

Title the role for the job. Not for the ambition.

New Generation Faces Changing Job Security - Adapt, Upskill, and Future-Proof Careers

Your Skills, Not Your Job Title, Define Your Career Security.

The reality of work is changing rapidly. Job security is no longer guaranteed, particularly in IT and outsourcing, where technological advances and flexible hiring practices have made careers less predictable. Contract, project-based, and temporary employment are becoming more common, while automation is reducing demand for repetitive tasks. Young professionals must therefore develop higher-value skills and remain prepared for continuous change.

To build a sustainable career, professionals need to upskill and reskill continuously, while developing resilience and adaptability. Technology evolves quickly, making some skills outdated. Learning to use AI effectively can improve productivity, automate routine work, and create more time for creativity, critical thinking, and decision-making. Professionals should also seek mentors, welcome constructive feedback, collaborate across teams, and build meaningful networks that can create future opportunities.

Organizations increasingly value people who can learn quickly, adapt to uncertainty, collaborate effectively, and deliver results under pressure. Experience remains valuable, but experience alone may not guarantee career security. Professionals who continuously update their knowledge, embrace new technologies, and remain flexible can better navigate changing employment conditions.

The future belongs not necessarily to those with the longest experience, but to those who never stop learning. Your greatest job security is your ability to adapt. Don’t wait for change to force you to act—start upskilling today and invest in yourself, because your skills are your strongest career asset.

Invest in your skills today—the future of work won’t wait.

🚨 STOP ASKING CHATGPT: “FIX MY CV.”

If you're using AI for your job search, the quality of your output often depends on the quality of your instructions.

Instead of asking ChatGPT to “make my CV better,” use prompts that force it to analyse, challenge, compare and improve specific parts of your application.

Here are 6 prompts worth saving 👇

1️⃣ THE CV X-RAY

«“Act as a senior recruiter in [industry]. Analyse my CV as if you are screening a real candidate. Identify weak sections, vague achievements and the biggest reason I could be rejected within seconds. Be direct and specific.”»

2️⃣ THE JD DECODER

«“Analyse this job description. Identify the skills explicitly stated, the capabilities likely expected but not clearly written, the critical keywords and what the hiring manager is actually trying to find.”»

3️⃣ THE ATS OPTIMISER

«“Compare my CV with this job description. Identify every meaningful gap in skills, terminology and experience. Rewrite relevant sections using accurate job-description terminology naturally—without keyword stuffing.”»

⚠️ Don't chase a fake “90+ ATS score.” Different ATS platforms evaluate documents differently, and there is no universal score.

4️⃣ THE ACHIEVEMENT TRANSFORMER

«“Rewrite each CV bullet to focus on impact rather than duties. Use: action + what I did + measurable result + business impact. If numbers are missing, suggest placeholders I can verify.”»

5️⃣ THE RECRUITER TEST

«“Review my CV as a recruiter screening candidates for this role. Identify what would immediately attract attention, what could create doubt, and which information needs to become more prominent.”»

6️⃣ THE FINAL CV AUDIT

«“Audit my final CV for ATS readability, relevance, keyword alignment, achievement quality, formatting, summary, skills and length. For every weakness, give me the precise change required.”»

🧠 THE BIGGER LESSON

AI isn't necessarily most useful when you ask it to write everything for you.

It becomes much more valuable when you use it as a structured reviewer, challenger and editing partner.

Think:

Analyse → Diagnose → Rewrite → Verify → Refine.

And one important rule:

NEVER INVENT ACHIEVEMENTS.

If AI suggests a metric, title, responsibility or accomplishment you cannot substantiate, verify it—or remove it.

Your CV represents your professional record.

AI should strengthen the presentation of your experience, not manufacture the experience.
